 Release Date: October 29, 2026

 Positive Points 
 Coastal Financial Corp ( NASDAQ:CCB ) returned to profitability in Q3 2026 with net income of $13.8 million, or $0.89 per diluted share, compared to a net loss of $42.1 million in the prior quarter. 
 BAS program fee income grew 17.6% quarter-over-quarter and 79.6% year-over-year to $14.1 million, reflecting the strength and stability of the broader partner portfolio. 
 The company ended the quarter well capitalized with a common equity Tier 1 ratio of 11.5%, up from 10.86% in the prior quarter. 
 Coastal Financial Corp ( NASDAQ:CCB ) identified over $20 million in potential annualized savings in non-interest expenses, expected to be achieved over the next four to six quarters. 
 Credit metrics in the specific partner portfolio improved, with annualized net charge-offs decreasing to 9.81% from 11.46% in the prior quarter, and loans 30+ days past due declining to 3.41% from 4.06%. 
 Negative Points 
 The company recorded a $46 million provision for credit losses in Q3 2026, including $43.9 million for BAS loans, largely offset by $41.8 million of credit enhancements, but still a significant expense. 
 A $3.1 million portion of the provision was not offset by credit enhancement income because collection was not considered probable, impacting earnings. 
 The specific partner portfolio had $511 million in loans outstanding, with a $22.8 million specific allowance unchanged from the prior quarter, and expected charge-offs by year-end. 
 Net interest margin declined to 6.59% from 7.27% in the prior quarter, primarily due to a shift in loan mix and tighter underwriting standards. 
 The company faces potential disruption from the acquisition of partner BlueVine by Valley National Bancorp, with $452.4 million in on-balance sheet deposits and $1.85 billion swept off-balance sheet, though no material adverse effect is expected.

 Q : Based on what you've seen since the second quarter, has the probability of recovering some of the provision and/or credit enhancement valuation adjustment improved, deteriorated, or remained broadly unchanged? A : Eric Sprink (CEO) said the recovery outlook has materially stayed the same. The company remains in open dialogue with the partner and is monitoring the portfolio closely. Past dues and charge-offs are improving, but rising interest rates affected the CECL models on the fixed-rate portfolio by extending weighted average lives, which drove a $3.1 million provision not offset by credit enhancement income because collection was not deemed probable. 
 Story Continues Q : On the $20 million in annualized savings, should expenses step down further in the fourth quarter, and is the benefit fairly linear? Is there an efficiency ratio target for 2027? A : Chris Adams (Executive Chairman) said the company is confident in the potential $20 million in savings, but the work has just started. The team is scrutinizing vendors, contractors, and internal duplication, and will continue that work in the fourth quarter while providing updates on how it flows to the P&L. He declined to give ratio projections for 2027. 
 Q : Is the $20 million a gross or net number, and should we expect a true $20 million drop in the run rate over four to six quarters, or is there reinvestment to contemplate? A : Chris Adams (Executive Chairman) confirmed it is a pre-tax number and that there could be reinvestment at different stages as the business is evaluated. However, from the vendor, contractor, and duplication side, the company expects to see that run rate over the next four to six quarters, so the analyst's framing is probably correct. 
 Q : How does losing the BlueVine relationship impact net revenue or net earnings, and is there risk of similar actions within the current partner base? A : Eric Sprink (CEO) said ownership changes are not surprising in a maturing fintech ecosystem and Coastal has been a direct beneficiary of such changes over time. The company is not aware of any other bank charter or ownership events today. On BlueVine specifically, Coastal has plenty of funding alternatives to sweep deposits back on balance sheet, and the company has not finalized the net income impact, weighing reduced oversight costs against potential reinvestment. 
 Q : Has there been any shift in how you manage partner credit, specifically the credit enhancement asset versus a harder dollar cash pledge or deposit guarantee? A : Eric Sprink (CEO) said Coastal is a learning organization that will continually update how it evaluates partners' indemnification ability, including liquidity, cash pledge accounts, and partner earnings. The diversity of partners' revenue streams versus monoline fintechs has become an internal focus, with the goal of improving the assessment framework over time. 
 Q : CCBX loan balances were down a little this quarter. Should we expect loan portfolio growth out of CCBX going forward, or are we in a period of continued remix? A : Eric Sprink (CEO) cautioned against reading too much into quarter-end balances, noting average balances were up $300 million. Coastal sold a larger-than-normal block of on-balance sheet credit cards during the quarter, reflecting partner and Coastal risk tolerances. He reiterated that Coastal remains a growth company with a robust pipeline, new products, and new partners coming online. 
 Q : How has efficiency improved over the last year in onboarding and servicing partners due to AI investments, and can you continue onboarding new partners while achieving cost discipline? A : Eric Sprink (CEO) said AI is mainly deployed in oversight, compliance, and anti-money laundering rather than onboarding. COO Tara Herger continues to refine team techniques, and the pipeline has been more rationalized to support consistent earnings. He said the company is balancing growth with appropriate oversight and controls. 
 Q : Can you break down the provision on the specific partner between loan growth versus macro changes in the CECL model, and what drove the charge-offs? A : Eric Sprink (CEO) said loan growth was nominal ($507 million to $511 million) and did not drive provisioning. The main driver was macro rate changes affecting prepayment speeds and extending weighted average lives under the WARM method, which extends lifetime losses in CECL. Charge-offs declined dramatically quarter over quarter and year over year, and delinquency trends are improving. 
 Q : Should we expect a smaller but modest amount of provision expense each quarter as the CECL model moves forward and you originate new loans? A : Eric Sprink (CEO) declined to give pro forma guidance but said the company will evaluate the matter every quarter. The partner is extremely cooperative, and the company is working with investment bankers, potential investors, accounting, finance, and credit teams, with board oversight, to assess all options. 
 Q : The core NIM in CCBX has moved higher the last two quarters while gross loan yields moved down. How much is loan and program mix versus better pricing? A : Eric Sprink (CEO) attributed the dynamic to mix, noting cash-secured installment loans grew $50 million to about $265 million and carry lower gross yields than unsecured cards. Both Coastal and its partners are tightening underwriting, which is showing up in lower charge-offs, lower delinquencies, and lower gross yields while net yield to Coastal is maintained. 
 Q : How much additional revenue can the existing platform support without another meaningful increase in spending? A : Chris Adams (Executive Chairman) said the platform has been built over a number of years and he sees no limitation on the growth side. The current focus is turning off older vendors, eliminating duplication, and building a leaner organization focused on efficiency and profitability while remaining a growth company. 
 Q : You had a big step-up in credit cards sold this quarter. How has the market's appetite for that paper changed? A : Eric Sprink (CEO) said the company executed a very large and successful transaction with one of its partners during the quarter. The market is liquid and able to absorb the paper, and Coastal maintains liquidity and capital buffers in case of a slowdown. He has not heard pushback that secondary markets are not operating efficiently.
